sentence: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor, a group of medicines used mainly to treat high blood pressure and sometimes heart failure and kidney problems.
note: NHS: ACE inhibitor used mainly for high blood pressure, sometimes heart failure and kidney problems.

sentence: The NHS says most adults and children aged 6 years and over can take it.
note: NHS who-can-take summary: most adults and children aged 6 and over can take lisinopril.

sentence: For high blood pressure, heart failure and kidney disease linked to diabetes, treatment is usually long term and can continue for the rest of a person's life.
note: NHS how-and-when: long-term treatment, even for life, for high blood pressure, heart failure and diabetic kidney disease.

sentence: Stopping it can let blood pressure rise, which can raise the chance of a heart attack or stroke, so the NHS advises speaking to a doctor before stopping.
note: NHS: stopping may cause blood pressure to rise, increasing chance of heart attack or stroke; talk to doctor first.

sentence: Lisinopril widens the blood vessels, which lowers blood pressure and eases the work the heart has to do.
note: NHS: works by making blood vessels widen, lowering blood pressure; common questions say it eases the heart's pumping work.

sentence: Blood pressure can start to fall within hours, but the full effect may take a few weeks.
note: NHS common questions: blood pressure can start falling within hours; full effect may take a few weeks.

sentence: The tablets are swallowed whole with a drink of water, with or without food, and the NHS suggests taking them at the same time each day.
note: NHS how-and-when: swallow whole with water; with or without food; same time every day.

sentence: Treatment often starts low and is increased gradually, and a doctor may suggest taking the first one at bedtime because it can cause dizziness.
note: NHS: doses usually start low and may be increased gradually; doctor may suggest first dose at bedtime because of dizziness.

sentence: Common side effects include headaches, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, dizziness and a dry cough that does not go away.
note: NHS side effects: headaches, feeling/being sick, diarrhoea, dizziness, dry persistent cough listed as common.

sentence: Dizziness is more likely when starting lisinopril or moving to a higher amount, and the NHS advises not to drive until it passes.
note: NHS: dizziness more likely at start or after an increase; do not drive until it passes.

sentence: If side effects bother you, a doctor may be able to offer a different medicine, so it is better not to stop it on your own.
note: NHS: doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine; do not stop on your own because blood pressure may rise.

sentence: Call 999 now if your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, if your throat feels tight, or if you struggle to swallow or breathe, which can be angioedema.
note: NHS: call 999 now for sudden swelling of lips, mouth, throat or tongue, tight throat, difficulty swallowing or breathing; angioedema named in the overview search summary.

sentence: Kidney problems are also listed, and blood tests check for them.
note: NHS: kidney problems listed as common; blood tests check for them.

sentence: Signs to watch for include swollen ankles, blood in your pee, or not peeing at all, and a GP or NHS 111 can advise on getting checked.
note: NHS lists these signs; the route to care (GP or NHS 111) was not stated in the returned text, added as a general pointer - reviewer to confirm against the page.

sentence: Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes can be a sign of liver problems and may be harder to see on brown or black skin.
note: NHS: yellow skin/eyes can be a sign of liver problems; harder to see on brown or black skin.

sentence: Alcohol can add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect and cause dizziness or light-headedness.
note: NHS: alcohol can increase blood pressure-lowering effect, dizziness, light-headedness.

sentence: The NHS advises avoiding it in the first few days or after an increase, until you see how the medicine affects you.
note: NHS common questions: avoid alcohol during first few days or after a dose increase.

sentence: The NHS says not to use salt substitutes such as Lo-Salt, because they are high in potassium and may push the potassium level in the blood too high.
note: NHS: do not use salt substitutes such as Lo-Salt; high in potassium; may make blood potassium too high with lisinopril.

sentence: The UK patient leaflet gives the same caution for potassium supplements and potassium-sparing water tablets such as spironolactone, triamterene and amiloride.
note: Search summary of UK leaflet: potassium supplements (incl. salt substitutes), potassium-sparing diuretics and other medicines that raise potassium; examples named in the summary.

sentence: It also lists anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) used for pain and arthritis as medicines to discuss with a doctor.
note: UK leaflet lists NSAIDs used to treat pain and arthritis among medicines to tell the doctor about.

sentence: The product information says that combining the two may increase the risk of worsening kidney function and raise potassium, especially when kidney function is already poor.
note: SmPC: combination may lead to increased risk of worsening renal function, possible acute renal failure, and increase in serum potassium, especially with poor pre-existing renal function.

sentence: If you have a high temperature, sweats, shaking, or severe diarrhoea or vomiting, the NHS says to contact your doctor, who may tell you to stop lisinopril until you recover.
note: NHS common questions: contact doctor with high temperature, sweats, shaking or severe diarrhoea/vomiting; may be told to stop until recovered.

sentence: The NHS lists several groups who may not be able to take lisinopril, including people who have had an allergic reaction to it or another medicine.
note: NHS who-can-and-cannot-take: allergic reaction to lisinopril or any other medicine.

sentence: The list also includes people with heart, liver or kidney problems, diabetes, unstable or low blood pressure, or those having dialysis.
note: NHS list per search summary: heart, liver or kidney problems, diabetes, unstable or low blood pressure, dialysis.

sentence: The UK patient leaflet says lisinopril must not be taken when more than three months pregnant, because it may seriously harm the baby after the third month.
note: UK leaflet (search summary): must not be taken when more than 3 months pregnant; may cause serious harm to baby after third month.

sentence: Doctors will normally advise stopping before pregnancy, or as soon as it is known, and switching to another medicine.
note: UK leaflet (search summary): doctor will normally advise stopping before becoming pregnant or as soon as pregnancy known and use another medicine.

sentence: A dry cough that does not go away is one of the common side effects of lisinopril.
note: NHS: dry persistent cough listed as common.

sentence: The NHS says it can take up to a month to clear after the medicine is stopped.
note: NHS: cough may take up to a month to go away after stopping.

sentence: If the cough bothers you, a doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine, so it is better to ask before stopping, because blood pressure can rise if lisinopril is stopped.
note: NHS: doctor may offer different medicine; stopping may cause blood pressure to rise.

sentence: Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, a tight throat, or difficulty swallowing or breathing needs a 999 call straight away.
note: NHS: call 999 now for these symptoms.

sentence: The NHS says angioedema, a form of sudden swelling, is more likely in people with black skin, so knowing the signs matters.
note: NHS summary: higher chance of angioedema with black skin.

sentence: The NHS says not to use salt substitutes such as Lo-Salt, because they are high in potassium and may push the potassium level in the blood too high.
note: NHS: do not use salt substitutes such as Lo-Salt; high in potassium.

sentence: The UK patient leaflet lists anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) among medicines to discuss with a doctor, and the product information says combining them may worsen kidney function.
note: Leaflet lists NSAIDs; SmPC says combination may increase risk of worsening renal function.

sentence: The NHS lists being pregnant, trying to get pregnant and breastfeeding among the situations where lisinopril may not suit someone.
note: NHS who-can-and-cannot-take lists pregnant, trying for pregnancy or breastfeeding.

sentence: The UK patient leaflet says it must not be taken when more than three months pregnant, and a doctor will normally advise switching to another medicine before pregnancy or as soon as it is known.
note: UK leaflet: must not be taken more than 3 months pregnant; doctor will normally advise stop and switch.
